items.title: Sweden tops global media freedom support rankings as international funding declines
items.desc: Sweden has been ranked the world's leading supporter of international media freedom, according to a new index. The index also highlights a decline in funding from 30 leading donor countries, despite growing threats to independent journalism worldwide.

items.title: Giant deer bones may push human arrival in Ireland back by 1,000 years
items.desc: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered tantalizing new evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago—nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

items.title: Fermented milk may have held ritual power in Neolithic Denmark
items.desc: Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

items.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
items.desc: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

items.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
items.desc: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. Meeting the demand for protein is taxing on the environment, requiring massive amounts of land and water while creating greenhouse gas emissions. And that demand is expected to require nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050 than in 2012, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization.

items.title: Draining peatlands leaves a long legacy of warming
items.desc: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. Although methane is a potent greenhouse gas, peatlands exhibit a net cooling effect on the planet because of the sheer scale of carbon dioxide they remove from the atmosphere, which has amounted to hundreds of gigatons globally over thousands of years.

items.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
items.desc: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. Researchers from the University of Jyväskylä have now identified more than 300 stable metallene sandwich structures using machine learning and high-performance computing. The results provide researchers with a practical roadmap for the fabrication of new two-dimensional metals.

items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
items.desc: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
items.desc: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

items.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
items.desc: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

items.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
items.desc: It's 7 a.m. Still dark outside. "Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

items.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
items.desc: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

items.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
items.desc: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for the science-gathering that lies ahead.

items.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
items.desc: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

items.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
items.desc: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

items.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
items.desc: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.desc: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.desc: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.desc: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
items.desc: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.desc: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.desc: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.desc: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
items.desc: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.desc: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
items.desc: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.desc: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

items.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
items.desc: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
items.desc: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

items.title: Who Can Speak for Europe in Peace Talks with Russia?
items.desc: The European Union's inability to find one person to represent it in such negotiations reflects a structural failure, not a shortage of skilled personnel. That is why the EU should step aside and delegate the selection of an envoy to the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.

items.title: The Fossil-Fuel Endgame Doesn’t Require a COP Consensus
items.desc: Despite the failure of this year's United Nations climate talks, there is no doubt that phasing out fossil fuels is the right goal. The only question is whether a coalition of the willing can use policy to push markets toward a faster, fairer, and smoother transition than the traditional COP process can deliver.

items.title: Who Controls America’s AI Chokepoint?
items.desc: The saga of Jensen Huang's ouster and sudden return as Nvidia's chief executive has exposed a paradox at the heart of American technological hegemony. While Nvidia's AI chips give the United States leverage over China, the geopolitical power that Nvidia makes possible gives it leverage over the US.

items.title: Where Development Cooperation Still Lives
items.desc: By helping developing economies build the capacity and infrastructure trade requires, the World Trade Organization's Aid for Trade initiative has contributed to a significant increase in these countries' share of global exports over the past 20 years. But the trade landscape is changing fast, and Aid for Trade must adapt.

items.title: Nvidia’s Liability Problem Isn’t Going Away
items.desc: Given previous suspicions about Nvidia's engagement with China, one wonders if Jensen Huang’s admitted extramarital affairs are just a cover-up for more consequential violations and misrepresentations. Whatever the case, the problem is not limited to Huang; with his reinstatement as CEO, it involves the company's entire board.

items.title: Mapping Strategic Supply-Chain Risk
items.desc: If there is a premium to be paid for resilient supply chains, who will foot the bill? The answer can be found through a three-stage approach of identifying current vulnerabilities, letting markets and public tenders price them, and then having national-security authorities intervene only where market pricing fails.

items.title: Holiday 2026 Reading List
items.desc: In the bi-weekly PS Book Recommendations newsletter —available for free to all registered PS readers—we highlight insightful, informative, or otherwise compelling books, written or recommended by PS contributors. Here, we present a selection of recent works by PS contributors that are worth adding to your holiday shopping list (and your bookshelf).

items.title: The Summit of Self-Promotion
items.desc: Despite claiming that world history was made in Shenzhen with the US–Russia–China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, the trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin was about optics, not substance. One of the many important problems they failed to address was China’s export-led growth.

items.title: Why Nvidia Couldn’t Quit Jensen Huang
items.desc: Developing AI requires tremendous coordination across firms and sectors, from the AI labs themselves to energy and computing infrastructure, as well as long-term vision and patience. Whereas much of this coordination and planning is led by the government in China, in the US, it has been driven largely by one CEO.

items.title: Chips Too Big to Fail
items.desc: The Trump administration pushed for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia to keep the stock market high, to feed a possible productivity surge, and to advance a US foreign policy built on reconciliation with China. But will Americans continue to believe in the AI miracle and this new version of Chimerica?

items.title: Amplifying the Voice of Human Limits
items.desc: Tech leaders like Elon Musk have embraced Prometheus as a symbol of creation, conquest, and discovery. But the Promethean impulse must be balanced by the “Orphic” tradition’s respect for and contemplation of nature’s mystery.

items.title: Making the Most of South Korea’s Semiconductor Boom
items.desc: The AI boom has driven South Korea’s economic growth well above expectations, thanks to soaring demand for advanced semiconductors. But AI’s transformative potential does not guarantee that the current investment frenzy will continue, leaving the economy vulnerable to a downturn.

items.title: Is a Financial-Market Reckoning Imminent?
items.desc: After a year of unprecedented AI investment, increasingly financed by debt in opaque private markets, growing unease about the industry’s future is reflected in sharp declines in the NASDAQ index and the S&P 500. But the stock market’s dependence on a handful of highly leveraged companies—and even a single CEO—is hardly the only source of global financial risk. Amid mounting fears, we asked PS contributors what to expect from financial markets in the year ahead.

items.title: The African Union’s Elusive Quest for Security
items.desc: The African Union has long sought to implement Ali Mazrui’s concept of Pax Africana, but has faced persistent logistical and financial constraints. The key to making peacekeeping operations more effective is establishing a better division of labor between the AU, the United Nations, and regional African organizations.

items.title: The Achilles’ Heel of Emerging Economies’ Trade
items.desc: New research shows that 23% of global goods imports in 2024 faced at least two of three vulnerabilities: product criticality, supply concentration, and geopolitical distance. Given the wide range of problems, early diagnosis and targeted action are particularly important for emerging economies with limited fiscal space.

items.title: Judge the Cyber Apocalypse by the Data, Not the Headlines
items.desc: The technical metrics on AI for cybersecurity now indicate that recent advances are enabling attackers more than defenders and that AI is regularly being used in attacks. This is in line with daily news stories on the “vulnpocalypse” and “Black October.” Surprisingly though, data on real-world impacts of cyber attacks tells a less dire story. If this trend continues, it could indicate that attribution and punishment matter at least as much as attackers’ technical capabilities. items.title: Biodata Matters for the Genesis Mission
items.desc: The Genesis Mission aims to harness artificial intelligence to supercharge scientific innovation and support the United States’ technological leadership, including in biotechnology. Accomplishing this goal requires lots of diverse, high-quality biological data, and the Mission plans to pull together federal datasets accordingly. This piece describes the categories of biodata challenges that the Genesis Mission is likely to face and makes recommendations about how to approach them. The article discusses how the proposed MATCH Act could affect Dutch chipmaking equipment manufacturer ASML and create tensions between the United States and its European allies.
